Zooming In On Mercari's Earnings

Many investors haven't heard of the accrual ratio from cashflow, but it is actually a useful measure of how well a company's profit is backed up by free cash flow (FCF) during a given period. To get the accrual ratio we first subtract FCF from profit for a period, and then divide that number by the average operating assets for the period. The ratio shows us how much a company's profit exceeds its FCF.

That means a negative accrual ratio is a good thing, because it shows that the company is bringing in more free cash flow than its profit would suggest. That is not intended to imply we should worry about a positive accrual ratio, but it's worth noting where the accrual ratio is rather high. That's because some academic studies have suggested that high accruals ratios tend to lead to lower profit or less profit growth.

Mercari has an accrual ratio of 0.57 for the year to September 2026. Statistically speaking, that's a real negative for future earnings. And indeed, during the period the company didn't produce any free cash flow whatsoever. Even though it reported a profit of JP¥40.6b, a look at free cash flow indicates it actually burnt through JP¥79b in the last year. It's worth noting that Mercari generated positive FCF of JP¥14b a year ago, so at least they've done it in the past.

Examining Cashflow Against WorkmanLtd's Earnings

One key financial ratio used to measure how well a company converts its profit to free cash flow (FCF) is the accrual ratio. The accrual ratio subtracts the FCF from the profit for a given period, and divides the result by the average operating assets of the company over that time. The ratio shows us how much a company's profit exceeds its FCF.

Therefore, it's actually considered a good thing when a company has a negative accrual ratio, but a bad thing if its accrual ratio is positive. That is not intended to imply we should worry about a positive accrual ratio, but it's worth noting where the accrual ratio is rather high. That's because some academic studies have suggested that high accruals ratios tend to lead to lower profit or less profit growth.

For the year to September 2026, WorkmanLtd had an accrual ratio of 0.22. Unfortunately, that means its free cash flow fell significantly short of its reported profits. In fact, it had free cash flow of JP¥8.8b in the last year, which was a lot less than its statutory profit of JP¥23.6b. LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton still asks shareholders to believe in global appetite for high end brands and in the group’s ability to turn that demand into steady cash generation. According to Ivoed, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community, the issue today is less the quality of the franchises and more whether a slower luxury cycle justifies the current price.

The recent appointment of a Chief Digital & Innovation Officer looks important for execution but does not obviously change the near term swing factors. The key upside catalyst remains evidence that Fashion & Leather Goods can regain momentum. The biggest near term risk is prolonged margin and valuation pressure if that profit engine stays soft.

Among the recent disclosures, the November update on LVMH share transactions is the most relevant here. It reinforces that investors are already tracking capital flows around the stock at a time when the share price is down roughly 35% over 1 year and trades below one internal future cash flow estimate of €444.63 per share.

That share transaction report sits next to the digital leadership reshuffle as another execution checkpoint for readers watching catalysts. Analysts as a group expect earnings to grow 8.69% a year and see upside of about 25.4% from current levels, yet the recovery path still depends on LVMH converting its data, omnichannel and brand investments into firmer demand in Fashion & Leather Goods.

Ivoed’s narrative lands on a fair value of €525.00 per LVMH share by pairing projected revenue growth of 9.5% a year with a future profit margin of 13.5%. That combination supports a view that cash generation and earnings quality can justify the 12 month base case target.

data.title: Why Computacenter (LSE:CCC) Could Be 26% Below Fair Value Following Guidance Upgrade
data.description:
Computacenter (LSE:CCC) has drawn fresh attention after management flagged sizeable order backlogs and upgraded profit guidance, prompting investors to reassess how its founder influenced, long tenured leadership might support future cash generation.

Recent trading in Computacenter has been choppy, with the share price up 2.69% on the day to £47.34 but down 4.83% over the past week and 6.90% over 90 days. At the same time, the year to date share price return of 62.12% and 1 year total shareholder return of 68.36% point to strong longer term momentum that recent profit guidance upgrades and order backlog comments have brought back into focus.

Computacenter looks like a robust, founder influenced IT services engine, yet the share price has already moved sharply on upgraded guidance. Is this still a solid business at a fair price, or now a quality premium?

Price-to-Earnings of 24.3x: Is it justified for Computacenter?

On a P/E of 24.3x, Computacenter trades at a level that sits between fair value models suggesting upside and sector benchmarks that look cheaper, which leaves the current £47.34 share price in a grey zone for valuation judgement.

The P/E ratio compares what you pay today to the earnings the business generates per share. For a mature IT services provider like Computacenter, this measure often reflects how much investors are willing to pay for its earnings quality, growth profile and cash conversion potential rather than just headline revenue size.

Computacenter is flagged as good value versus its estimated fair P/E of 35.1x and is also marked as trading 25.9% below an internal future cash flow estimate. This points to the market putting a lower tag on its earnings than that model suggests could be justified. At the same time, the share trades above the broader European IT industry on 17.6x and only roughly in line with a 25x peer average, which shows investors are already paying a clear premium that the market could, over time, either lean into or push back against if expectations change.
